title: Building tools: web search, calculator, file access
notes: Web search can be a server tool: add web_search to the tools list and Anthropic runs it, returning results with sources.
Models are unreliable at exact arithmetic, so give them a calculator that parses with ast and never calls eval.
A file tool opens files only inside one allowed folder, and refuses paths like ../ that climb out of it.

slides.title: Building tools: web search, calculator, file access
slides.sub: Three tools almost every agent needs, and how to keep each one safe
sentences: Now that you can define a tool, let us build some.
In this lesson you will meet three tools almost every agent needs: web search, a calculator and a file reader.
For each one you will see what it is for, and the one mistake that makes it dangerous.

slides.title: Three tools, three gaps
sentences: Each of these tools fills a gap the model has on its own.
The model's knowledge stops when its training did, so web search lets it look up what is happening now.
For Scout, that might be a storm closing a ParcelPath depot this week.
Models are also surprisingly unreliable at exact arithmetic, so a calculator does the sums.
Scout needs that for discounts and refunds, where one cent out means a complaint.
And the model has never seen your documents, so a file reader lets it open Orbit's policy.

slides.title: Web search: a tool you don't run yourself
slides.lead: Web search is a server tool: Anthropic runs it. You only add one entry to the tools list.

rows.out: A tool Anthropic hosts, not your code
At most three searches per request
Results arrive in the same response

aside.label: Worth knowing
aside.text: Each search costs extra and adds time. Turn it on only where Scout really needs fresh facts.

sentences: Web search is the easiest of the three, because you do not run it yourself.
It is a server tool: you add a small entry with a type, and Anthropic runs the search on its side.
Max uses caps how many searches the model may make in one request, and three is plenty for Scout.
You add it to the same tools list as your own tools.
The searches and their results come back inside the same response, with links to the sources, so your loop never has to run anything.
If you already pay for a search service, you can wrap its API as an ordinary tool instead.
Either way, searches cost money and add time, so turn web search on only where Scout needs fresh facts.

slides.title: Why give a language model a calculator?

left.label: In its head
points: Sounds just as sure either way
One cent out is a refund complaint

sentences: Why would a model that writes so well need a calculator?
Because it predicts digits much like words, so easy sums usually come out right, and harder ones sometimes don't.
The worrying part is that it sounds just as sure either way.
For refunds and discounts, one cent out is a complaint, or money lost.
With a calculator tool, the model writes the expression, and your code works it out exactly.
The model does what it is good at, choosing the right sum and explaining it, and Python does the arithmetic.

slides.title: A safe calculator: parse it, never eval it
slides.lead: Never pass model text to eval. Parse it with ast, and allow only numbers and arithmetic.

rows.out: Never: runs any Python the text contains
Text becomes a tree; nothing runs

aside.label: The rule
aside.text: Treat every tool input as untrusted text, even when it comes from your own agent.

sentences: Here is the one mistake that makes a calculator dangerous.
Python's eval function would happily work out the sum, but it runs any Python the text contains.
If a customer talks Scout into calculating a line of code that deletes files, eval would run it.
Instead, use Python's ast module to parse the text into a tree, which runs nothing at all.
Then walk the tree and allow only numbers, the four basic operations, powers and parentheses.
Anything else, such as a name, a function call or an import, is refused with a clear error.
Treat every tool input as untrusted text, even when it comes from your own agent.

slides.title: A file reader that stays in its folder

note.text: read_file("../.env") resolves outside docs, so it is refused before anything is opened.

sentences: The file reader lets Scout open Orbit's documents, and only those.
Scout asks for a file by name, such as the policy file.
Your code joins that name to the docs folder and resolves it into a full, absolute path.
Then it checks that the result is still inside docs, and refuses if it is not.
That stops tricks like dot dot slash, which climbs out of the folder towards your code and your API keys.
Only then does it read the file and send the text back to Scout.

slides.title: How much power should a tool get?

cells: ast and an allow-list of operators
Resolve the path, check it's inside

note.text: Least privilege: give each tool the least power that still does the job.

sentences: Put the three side by side and a pattern appears.
Web search reaches the public web, so you cap it and switch it on only where it is needed.
The calculator reaches numbers only, guarded by an allow-list of operators.
The file reader reaches one folder, guarded by the path check.
Compare a tool that runs any Python the model writes: it reaches everything, and there is no simple guard.
The principle is called least privilege: give each tool the least power that still does the job.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: web_search is a server tool: add it to the list, Anthropic runs it
Give the model a calculator; parse with ast, never eval
File access stays in one folder; resolve and check every path
Least privilege: each tool gets only the power it needs

sentences: Let us pull it together.
Web search is a server tool: add it to your list, and Anthropic runs it for you.
Models are unreliable at exact sums, so give them a calculator that parses with ast and never calls eval.
A file tool stays inside one folder, and checks every path before it opens anything.
And every tool gets the least power that does its job.
In the guided practice, you will build the calculator and the file reader yourself.

midQuiz.q: Scout has the web_search tool in its list. Who runs the searches?
options: Your run_tool dispatcher, which calls a search API
Anthropic, on its servers; results come back in the same response
Nobody: the model answers from what it learned in training
midQuiz.explain: web_search is a server tool. You add it to the tools list; Anthropic runs the search and returns results with their sources.
midQuiz.hint: Did you write a Python function for web search?

midQuiz.q: Why should calculate never pass the model's expression to eval?
options: eval is too slow for large numbers
eval runs any Python in the text, not just arithmetic
midQuiz.explain: eval executes code. Parsing with ast and allowing only arithmetic means nothing else can ever run.
midQuiz.hint: Besides sums, what else can one line of Python do?

endQuiz.q: Scout calls read_file with "../.env". What should happen?
options: Open it, because Scout asked for it
Refuse it: the resolved path is outside the docs folder
Remove the dots and open .env from inside docs
endQuiz.explain: Resolve the full path and check it is inside docs before opening anything. ../ climbs out of the folder, so the request is refused.
endQuiz.hint: Where does ../ point, compared with the docs folder?

endQuiz.q: Which tool design follows least privilege?
options: A run_python tool, so Scout can do anything it needs
A read_file tool that can open only files inside docs
A read_file tool that can open any path on the server
endQuiz.explain: Least privilege means each tool gets only the power its job needs. Scout only needs Orbit's documents, so read_file reaches docs and nothing else.
endQuiz.hint: Which option gives Scout the smallest reach that still does the job?
